claims.text: In-situ HRTEM equipped with an integrated heating stage can investigate the thermal behavior of AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles at near-atomic resolution.
AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles will exhibit minimal atomic-scale rearrangement or phase segregation up to high temperatures.
High configurational entropy confers enhanced thermal stability on AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles are nearly equiatomic and compositionally homogeneous.
The initial AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles constitute a high-entropy alloy.
Controlled in-situ heating to approximately 800°C under vacuum or inert conditions is an appropriate intervention for testing nanoparticle thermal stability.
Step-wise heating with controlled ramp rates and isothermal holds permits continuous near-atomic-resolution monitoring of structural evolution.
Relevant structural indicators include interatomic spacing, local lattice order, phase boundaries, and segregated regions.
Thermal energy can overcome kinetic barriers and cause atomic diffusion.
High configurational entropy should suppress significant phase separation or precipitation in a stable high-entropy alloy.
Insufficient entropy stabilization will lead to atomic reordering and segregation during heating.
Effective stabilization would allow the nanoparticles to remain largely homogeneous without significant phase segregation or morphological coarsening up to the tested temperatures.
Formation of segregated phases, substantial atomic rearrangement, or coarsening before the stability threshold would indicate instability.
The as-synthesized AuCoCuNiPt nanoparticles have a uniform single-phase structure with no discernible atomic-scale heterogeneity at room temperature.
TEM observations in the nanoparticle size regime may be influenced by electron-beam effects and surface phenomena and may not represent bulk high-temperature behavior.
HRTEM images can reveal atomic rearrangements, phase boundaries, segregated regions, and particle coarsening during heating.
SAED patterns can monitor phase evolution and identify the emergence of new phases during heating.
Observation of significant reordering, segregation, coarsening, or new diffraction phases below the predicted stability threshold would falsify the proposed entropy-stabilization hypothesis.
